results.title: The Cheapest GPU Rental Right Now (November 2026): What 'Cheapest' Actually Means for H100, H200, and B200
results.author: Dex Mareno
highlights:
The takeaway

- Entering November 2026, the cheapest GPU rental depends entirely on which 'cheapest' you mean: the marketplace/spot floor, a reliable named on-demand rate, or the market median — and they can differ by 2–4x on the same card.
- Cheapest reliable on-demand right now: H100 (80GB) ~$1.99–2.89/GPU-hr (Voltage Park ~$1.99, Thunder Compute ~$2.19, RunPod ~$2.89), H200 (141GB) ~$3.59–4.29 (RunPod ~$3.59, Crusoe ~$4.29), B200 (Blackwell) ~$5.50–6.99 (Lambda is the cheapest reliable on-demand B200).
- Marketplace/spot floors go lower and less certain: H100 asks from ~$1.74 (Vast.ai) and spot ~$1.03 (Spheron), H200 asks from ~$2.25–2.76, B200 single-provider floors as low as ~$3.69 but with availability and trust caveats.
- Market medians are much higher: ~$4.20 H100, ~$5.70 H200, ~$8.19 B200 (Uvik's October index) — so a random provider costs roughly double the floor.
- Hyperscalers (AWS/Azure/GCP) stay ~$7–14/hr for the identical card — you pay 3–6x for the platform, not the silicon.
- The real cheapest option is often NOT renting: below ~40–50% duty cycle a per-token API beats renting metal at any of these rates, because a rented GPU bills 24/7 whether it works or not.
- And the direction of travel just changed: with Microsoft and Google pausing capex and chip delays pushing capacity to H1 2027, the price floor that stopped falling in October is now firming — the cheapest rate you see today may be the cheapest you'll see for a while.

...

**The cheapest reliable on-demand rate right now (November 2026):**

- H100 (80GB) → ~$1.99–2.89/GPU-hr. Voltage Park ~$1.99, Thunder Compute ~$2.19, RunPod ~$2.89.
- H200 (141GB) → ~$3.59–4.29/hr. RunPod ~$3.59, Crusoe ~$4.29.
- B200 (Blackwell) → ~$5.50–6.99/hr. Lambda is typically the cheapest reliable on-demand Blackwell.

...

Through mid-2026, the rental floor fell most months — the rational move was to wait a month for a lower number. Last month's map noted the floor had gone flat. This month the direction turned slightly firmer, and the reason is supply, not demand.

Three of these need a note. CoreWeave and Azure price a whole 8-GPU machine by the hour: $49.24 and $98.32 for the H100. The per-GPU figures above are our own arithmetic. AWS publishes a plain on-demand rate only in its calculator, so the AWS row is its Capacity Blocks price, and for the H200 it is the p5e machine (the p5en costs $7.90). Google's row is the Vertex AI managed service, which is not the same product as a bare virtual machine.

Even so, the spread is wide. The H100 runs from $3.99 to $12.29, about three times. The B200 runs from $6.69 to $14.21, about twice. Rate cards also move. In our read on 8 October, Nebius showed $3.85 for an H100. On 3 November it showed $4.50.

## What commitments change

Every provider here says a commitment lowers the rate. Few publish by how much.

C Compute · published commitment discounts Read 3 Nov 2026

E2E Networks 10% to 30%, its own figure

Sakura Internet 5% for 6 months, 10% for 12

Each provider's own pages, read 3 Nov 2026. Discounts off list rates.

- CoreWeave says it offers up to 60% off its on-demand prices for committed use. That is its own claim. The page lists no committed rate.
- Azure publishes reservation prices through its public price API. For the H100 machine in East US, the one-year price works out 36% below pay as you go and the three-year price 56% below. We divided each term price by its hours.
- Google Cloud lists Flexible Savings Plan rates on the Vertex AI page. For the H200 they are $9.64 for one year and $8.57 for three, which is 10% and 20% below $10.71.
- E2E Networks says three-month, six-month and annual commitments can earn 10% to 30%, depending on length and volume.
- Sakura Internet announced on 1 July 2026 a commitment plan for one H100 plan: 5% off for six months and 10% off for twelve.
- AWS cut P5 (H100) prices by 44% for on-demand and 45% for the three-year Instance Savings Plan from 1 June 2025. Those are cuts from its earlier prices, not discounts off today's rate.
- Nebius and Lambda name no percentage. Both point large buyers to sales.

## Hyperscalers

On-demand prices per GPU-hour at the largest clouds remain far above specialist clouds: H100 from $6.88 (8-GPU instance divided by eight) to more than $12 depending on the provider, and B300 from $15 to $17.80. Commitments of one to three years cut those prices by 30 to 56%.

## What moved in 2026

- Prices are rising again for flagships. At least one large specialist cloud announced increases of 10 to 26% on H100, H200 and B300 from December 1.

- Listed is not available. Several providers list GPUs with no deployable region, or “contact sales” for every flagship.
- Fees moved to storage and idle time. Egress is mostly free; stopped-instance storage, public IPs and minimum billing periods are where extra cost appears.

results.title: Nebius removes its spot-price ceiling — preemptible GPUs can now cost more than on-demand | GPUJournal
highlights:
In an update note dated Nov 2, 2026 on its own blog, Nebius says the cap that kept its dynamic spot price one cent below the on-demand rate is gone. Spot still has a floor — it just no longer has a top, and setting your own max price is now the only brake.

Image: Nebius via nebius.com

What changed, from Nebius's own post “Introducing spot pricing for preemptible VMs” (published Sep 22, 2026; read Nov 2, 2026): its update note, dated Nov 2, 2026, reads — “this section previously stated that the spot price always stays between a floor and a ceiling one cent below the on-demand rate. We have removed the ceiling. Customers can cap what they pay by setting a max price.” The post's how-it-works section now states plainly: “There is no upper limit, so during periods of high demand the spot price can rise above the on-demand GPU-hour rate.”

How the mechanism works, in the same post: the spot price for a GPU type in a region is set from available capacity and real-time demand, recalculated up to every 15 minutes, and it still cannot fall below a set floor — only the ceiling has gone. A renter who sets a max price keeps the old protection by hand: when spot rises above the cap, the instance stops, data is retained, and it can restart when the price falls back — automatically for Kubernetes clusters, manually (or via Terraform, SDK, API or CLI) for standalone VMs. A renter who instead chose to follow the spot price has no cap at all after today's change.

What did not change: Nebius's on-demand list. Re-read on Nebius's own prices page on Nov 2, 2026, B300 is $9.50 an hour, B200 $8.50, H200 $5.40, H100 $4.50, RTX PRO 6000 $1.80 and L40S from $1.55 — every figure the same as our Nov 1 read. This is not a price rise in the list; it is the removal of the guarantee that the interruptible lane is always the cheaper one.

...

A spot price that can pass the on-demand rate in a busy hour inverts that pitch exactly when capacity is tightest — which, in the autumn pattern this journal has been tracking (Nebius's own across-the-board rise on Oct 1, Verda's eight rises since Oct 23, SaladCloud's demand-cited rise on Nov 1), is more and more of the time.

...

If you rent preemptible VMs on Nebius, do one thing today: set a max price. The ceiling that used to do that job for you was removed on Nov 2, and a workload set to follow the spot price can now be billed above the on-demand rate in a high-demand hour — paying a premium for capacity that can still be reclaimed. The discount lane still exists, but from today the discount is something you enforce yourself.

results.title: Verda raises prices again — all nine GPUs up about 1%, the eighth rise since Oct 23 | GPUJournal
highlights:
Read on Verda's own pricing page today, Nov 2, 2026, against the figures read there on Nov 1: every GPU in Verda's range rose by about 1% — GB300, B300, B200, H200, H100, both A100s, the RTX PRO 6000 and the L40S. After two flat checks, the October rise run has resumed.

Image: Verda via verda.com

What changed, read on verda.com/pricing on Nov 2, 2026 (unrounded page figures in brackets): GB300 $13.05 → $13.18 [$13.18], B300 $11.35 → $11.46 [$11.46], B200 $8.87 → $8.96 [$8.958], H200 $6.25 → $6.31 [$6.313], H100 SXM $4.79 → $4.84 [$4.841], A100 80GB $2.25 → $2.27 [$2.270], A100 40GB $1.61 → $1.63 [$1.625], RTX PRO 6000 $2.65 → $2.67 [$2.671] and L40S $1.90 → $1.92 [$1.920]. Each move is within a cent of +1.0% — a uniform list adjustment, not one card repricing.

The pattern: Verda rose on Oct 23, 24, 26, 27, 28, 29 and 30, then held on Oct 31 and Nov 1 — and has now risen an eighth time.

...

What it costs: Verda holds the board's Best offer on only two cards — the GB300 and the A100 40GB — and both rose today, so those two best offers rose with it. Everywhere else the cheapest verified offers are other providers' and none moved: the board's H100 SXM best is still TensorDock at $2.25 an hour (at an 8-GPU minimum) and its B200 best is still RunPod Community at $5.98. If you rent at Verda around the clock, today's rise adds about $95 a month per GB300, $65 per B200 and $35 per H100 on a 730-hour month — small per hour, real per fleet.

...

For renters, the lesson of the Verda run is the spread, not the rise: list prices at the rising providers keep stepping up about 1% at a time while the market's best verified offers have not moved since mid-October. A workload priced off one provider's list page in October can be 10% adrift by November. Check the board before renewing or expanding at a list rate — and if you are on Verda's GB300 or A100 40GB, your best-offer price moved today.

results.title: GPU Loan Underwriting: What Lenders Actually Score ...
results.author: Samuel McCulloch
highlights:
On-demand revenue doesn't disqualify a deal in Compute IQ, and it is priced for its shorter commitment. Compute IQ's illustrative sample deal covers 256 NVIDIA B200 GPUs on a 36-month AI lab contract. The customer earns 34 points and the contract earns 36.

...

The loan has to amortize faster than the hardware loses value, and the rental rate drives both sides of that test. GPU depreciation and repayment capacity move together because both follow what the chips earn per hour. Silicon Data put its H100 neocloud index at $2.94 per GPU-hour on Nov 2, 2026. Silicon Data's B200 index read $6.64 per GPU-hour on Oct 31, 2026.
